1171.quote_or_event: “These are the very eyes which used to see the extremely beautiful form of the beloved Lord and satisfying their desire would absorb themselves in the spiritual bliss. ... These are the eyes that used to suffer the most at the time of separation of the Lord, the Master of my life.”
1171.explanation: Bhai Gurdas devotes a whole kabitt to the eyes: the same eyes that once feasted on the Beloved's form are the ones that suffer most when He is gone. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
1171.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her eyes showed her the beloved and so brought on her endless sickness, yet now they weep to see him; Bhai Gurdas likewise singles out the eyes as both the first to delight and the worst to suffer.
1171.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 669, English translation as given in the BaniDB database
1171._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (kabitt 669, lines 1 and 3 joined by an ellipsis); strong fit on the eyes as both source of joy and chief sufferers, though Bhai Gurdas does not blame the eyes as the Kural does, and the Beloved is the Lord.

1172.quote_or_event: “In a dream, He came, and went away again; I cried so many tears.”
1172.explanation: Guru Nanak's soul-bride glimpses the Husband Lord only in a dream, and when He is gone again she weeps.
1172.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her eyes once looked at her lover without a thought for what would follow, and now they suffer; Guru Nanak's bride likewise has a fleeting sight of the Beloved and is left in tears.
1172.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 558, Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1172._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable but partial: it shares a moment of sight followed by tears, but has none of the Kural's reproach of the eyes for looking rashly.

1173.quote_or_event: “I used to see my beloved Lord without a blink of the eye as a ruddy sheldrake looks at moon. There used to be no break. But now I don't even see Him in a dream.”
1173.explanation: Bhai Gurdas recalls how the lover's eyes once gazed at the Beloved without blinking, like the chakor bird at the moon, and now cannot glimpse Him even in dreams. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
1173.tie_back: The Kural's heroine laughs bitterly at eyes that rushed of their own accord to look at the beloved and now weep of their own accord; Bhai Gurdas sets the same contrast between the eyes' eager gazing then and their deprivation now.
1173.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 670, English translation as given in the BaniDB database
1173._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (kabitt 670, first line; the translation names the bird a ruddy sheldrake); next-best match: the eager-then, deprived-now contrast fits, but there is no mockery of the eyes, which is the point of the Kural.

1174.quote_or_event: “I cannot survive without seeing my Beloved. My eyes are welling up with tears.”
1174.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that without the sight of the Beloved he cannot live, and his eyes overflow with tears.
1174.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her eyes, having planted in her a sickness she cannot survive, have wept until no tears are left; Guru Ram Das likewise joins a longing he cannot survive to eyes running with tears.
1174.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 94, Raag Maajh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1174._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on deadly longing and weeping eyes, but the Kural's eyes are cried dry, while the Guru's are still welling, and his Beloved is the Guru and God.

1175.quote_or_event: “My eyes long for the Blessed Vision of Your Darshan; the night passes, but I cannot sleep.”
1175.explanation: Guru Arjan describes eyes that thirst for the sight of the Lord and so stay open through the whole night.
1175.tie_back: The Kural says the eyes that brought on a love-sickness greater than the sea are now tormented by being unable to sleep; Guru Arjan's eyes likewise long for the Beloved and cannot close all night.
1175.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 542, Raag Bihaagraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1175._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on sleepless, longing eyes, though Guru Arjan does not cast the eyes as the cause of the sickness, and the longing is for God.

1176.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, that human body, in which there is no pain of separation from the Lord-take that body and burn it.”
1176.explanation: Guru Angad says the pain of separation from the Lord is so precious that a body without it is worth only burning.
1176.tie_back: The Kural's heroine calls it sweet that the eyes which gave her this sickness have fallen into the same suffering; Guru Angad likewise treats the pain of separation as something to be welcomed rather than escaped.
1176.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 89, Sri Raag ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1176._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: both value the pain of longing, but the Kural's 'sweetness' is ironic satisfaction at the eyes' punishment, which has no counterpart in Gurbani.

1177.quote_or_event: “I cherish and remember that Friend; the eyes of this soul-bride are filled with tears.”
1177.explanation: Guru Nanak's soul-bride keeps remembering her divine Friend, and her eyes fill with tears as she does.
1177.tie_back: The Kural wishes that the eyes which once melted with longing as they gazed on him may ache until their tears run dry; Guru Nanak's bride remembers her Beloved with eyes that are full of tears.
1177.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1111, Raag Tukhaari, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1177._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the tear-filled eyes of longing, but the Kural's mock-curse on the eyes has no parallel, and the love is spiritual.

1178.quote_or_event: “My mind longs for the Blessed Vision of the Guru's Darshan. It cries out like the thirsty song-bird. My thirst is not quenched, and I can find no peace, without the Blessed Vision of the Beloved Saint.”
1178.explanation: Guru Arjan compares himself to the rain-bird (chatrik) crying for water: without the sight of his Beloved Guru, his thirst is never quenched and he has no peace.
1178.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her eyes cannot rest without seeing him even though he does not truly care for her; Guru Arjan likewise says he finds no peace at all without the sight of the beloved.
1178.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1178._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa, three consecutive lines); strong fit on finding no rest without seeing the beloved, though the Kural's complaint that he loves her without caring has no parallel, and Guru Arjan longs for the Guru.

1179.quote_or_event: “The pain of separation has grown shy, for I have obtained the Blessed Vision of His Darshan; His Ambrosial Glance of Grace has filled me with bliss.”
1179.explanation: Guru Arjan says that once the soul-bride has seen her Lord, the pain of separation slinks away and His glance fills her with bliss.
1179.tie_back: The Kural's eyes find no sleep either when he is away or when he comes, because even his presence brings fear of parting; in Gurbani, by contrast, the Beloved's arrival ends the pain of separation and brings rest.
1179.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 460, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1179._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match by contrast only: the Kural's point is that union itself is spoiled by dread of parting, which Gurbani does not share for union with the Lord.

1180.quote_or_event: “Just as the beat of the drum is heard on all four sides (its sound cannot be hidden) ... Similarly, the Guru-oriented Sikh whose heart is enlightened by the love of the Lord and His meditation, cannot remain hidden. His silence gives him away.”
1180.explanation: Bhai Gurdas says that love for the Lord cannot be hidden any more than a beaten drum can, and that even the lover's silence reveals it. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
1180.tie_back: The Kural says the town easily learns the secret of women whose eyes proclaim it like a beaten drum; Bhai Gurdas uses the same image of a drum heard on every side for love that cannot be concealed.
1180.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 411, English translation as given in the BaniDB database
1180._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (kabitt 411, first and last lines joined by an ellipsis); strong fit on love betrayed as by a beaten drum, though Bhai Gurdas does not name the eyes or tears, and the love is for the Lord.
